name: Emeka Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Dawson's, a free-range egg farm. Sixteen thousand hens in four sheds, and they go out onto the fields in the day. I start at six, walk every shed, check the water lines and the feeders, pick up the floor eggs, the ones laid in the litter instead of the nest boxes, and take out any dead birds. Then I help on the packing table until the lorry comes at eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet in the sheds before the lights come up, and I like that Mr Dawson trusts me with the keys. What wears me out is the smell in summer and the early starts in winter, in the dark, every single day, Christmas included. Hens don't know it's Sunday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Through church. Mr Dawson's an elder at our church, and when I left the bakery job three years ago he said come and try it. I'm still not quick, the older guys can walk a shed in half my time. I'm getting married next summer, to Grace, so I need to get better and get a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but I won't be using it. It's for people in offices. On the farm, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing to me. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't plan to. My grandfather kept chickens behind his house his whole life with no computer, and the hens laid fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Work hard, ask Mr Dawson about a raise in the spring, and keep saving for the wedding. We've got about three months of money put by, and most of that is meant for the wedding day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It doesn't touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Most of your savings are for the wedding. What happens if something goes wrong before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wedding gets smaller, that's all. Grace and I already said, the church hall is fine, we don't need a hotel. My mother would be upset, but she'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything on the farm that's already done by computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The egg grading machine counts and sorts by size, and the shed lights and fans are on timers. Mr Dawson's son set up an app for the temperature, but I don't touch it. I tell him if a shed feels wrong, and he checks his phone.

S0.say: I'd say good luck to them, but I won't be using it, because it's for office people. On the farm nothing changes.
S0.think: It means nothing to me, since I've never used AI and don't plan to. My grandfather kept chickens his whole life with no computer and the hens laid fine.
S0.do: Carries on working hard and asks Mr Dawson for a raise in spring. Keeps saving for the wedding, which takes most of his three months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, because it doesn't touch him.
S0.quote: I tell him if a shed feels wrong, and he checks his phone.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is rooted in church, family and a job he got through his community. He's comfortable with others using technology as long as he doesn't have to. The wedding is the centre of his plans and his savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if companies don't hire beginners, they'll have nobody in ten years, and that's their own foolishness. Young people need a start, like Mr Dawson gave me. I'd say it at church, where people would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm already in, so it's not my problem directly. But my younger brother leaves school next year, and if nobody hires beginners, what does he do? I don't want him sitting at home on benefits, that's no life for a young man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Dawson if my brother could come and work weekends, learn the hens like I did. I'd keep my head down and work hard. I'd maybe stop eating out on Fridays so the wedding money grows a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him nobody owes you a job, you go and ask, and you keep asking. That's what our dad told me. Then I'd drive him to Dawson's myself on Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's companies' own foolishness. Should government make them hire beginners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think government should force anyone. But it could make apprenticeships cheaper for small farms, so it's worth it for Mr Dawson to take someone on. Make work pay, that's how I'd put it.

S1.say: I'd say companies that don't hire beginners will have nobody in ten years, which is their own foolishness. Young people need a start, like I got, and people at church would agree.
S1.think: I'm already in, so it's not my problem directly, but my brother leaves school next year. I don't want him sitting at home on benefits, because that's no life for a young man.
S1.do: Asks Mr Dawson to take his brother on for weekend work and drives him there himself. Stops eating out on Fridays to grow the wedding fund faster.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for his brother.
S1.quote: I'd tell him nobody owes you a job, you go and ask, and you keep asking.
S1.fieldNote: His views come straight from his father and church: work, not handouts, and help through family. He'd rather government make apprenticeships cheaper than force firms. His worry is for his brother, and he'd act on it at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people losing office jobs should look at real work, farms, building, care, there's plenty to do. Government should help them retrain, not just pay them to stay home. Politicians arguing doesn't feed anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't affect me much. Grace works at the bank in town, on the counter, and banks have been cutting staff for years. I'd worry about her more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace to start looking now, before anything happens, maybe at the school or the surgery reception. We'd keep the wedding money where it is and not touch it. I'd ask Mr Dawson about more hours, Saturdays, so we have something extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For Grace, not for the hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say if you told her to start looking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, I'm not leaving a good job because of a story on the news. She's stubborn, like me. She'd probably be right, too, until she wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should look at real work. Is office work not real work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That came out wrong, maybe. It's real work, Grace does it. I just mean there are jobs with your hands that need people, and nobody wants to do them, so it seems strange to sit at home.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs should look at hands-on work like farms, building and care. Government should help them retrain, not pay them to stay home.
S2.think: It doesn't affect me much, but Grace works on the counter at the bank in town. Banks have been cutting staff for years, so I'd worry about her more than me.
S2.do: Urges Grace to start looking for work at the school or surgery reception and keeps the wedding fund untouched. Asks Mr Dawson for Saturday hours to bring in extra money.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Grace, not for the hens.
S2.quote: She'd probably be right, too, until she wasn't.
S2.fieldNote: His public line, that people should do real work, slipped into a dismissal of office work, and he corrected himself when I named it. His fiancée works in a bank, so the office threat is close to home. He trusts family to sort it, not politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep what they earn, but if lots of people lose jobs, then churches and families and communities have to step up. I don't want government taking everything and handing it out. I'd say that out loud, though some friends wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is safe in this one. But if house prices boom, Grace and I can't buy, and we wanted a little house near her mum after the wedding. If she loses her bank job too, we'd be living on my wage, which is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Mr Dawson and ask if there's any chance of the flat over the packing shed for a year or two. I'd work every Saturday he'd give me. And I'd move the wedding money into a separate account so we can't spend it on bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The job's fine, but the future we planned is shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said communities should step up. What would that look like in your church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already run a food bank on Thursdays. If lots of people lost jobs, we'd need more volunteers and more food. I'd probably give eggs, Mr Dawson already gives the cracked ones every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for the house prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people with all that money buying houses they don't live in, and the councils for not letting anyone build. It's not fair on young families. But I don't blame the market itself, that's how it works.

S3.say: I'd say people should keep what they earn, and if many lose jobs, churches, families and communities must step up. I don't want government taking everything and handing it out.
S3.think: My job is safe, but booming house prices mean Grace and I can't buy near her mum. If she lost her bank job too, my wage alone wouldn't be enough.
S3.do: Asks Mr Dawson about the flat over the packing shed for a year or two and works every Saturday offered. Moves the wedding money into a separate account so it can't go on bills.
S3.feel: Anxious: the job is fine but the future they planned is shaky.
S3.quote: I'd probably give eggs, Mr Dawson already gives the cracked ones every week.
S3.fieldNote: He holds to free-market views but blames investors and councils for house prices. His answer to a crisis is the church food bank, which is already running. He sees community as the real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, slow it down, and think about families before we put robots everywhere. People need work, it's how you feed a family and how you keep your dignity. I'd say it at church and to anyone who listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. There's already a robot that drives round the shed floor and picks up the floor eggs, Mr Dawson's son showed me a video and laughed. That's half my morning, and I'm the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray about it first, honestly, and then I'd talk to Mr Dawson man to man and ask him what he's planning. I'd save everything, even push the wedding back if I had to. And I'd look at jobs where you need a person, maybe lorry driving, or back to the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground I stood on isn't mine any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run the robot, if Mr Dawson asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try. I'd be bad at it, I'm bad with phones even. But if it's that or the job, I'd sit with his son every evening until I got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing the wedding back. What would that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt more than losing the job, honestly. Grace's dad would ask why, and I'd have to say I can't promise I can keep her. That's the conversation I'd dread most.

S4.say: I'd say slow down and think about families before putting robots everywhere. Work is how you feed a family and keep your dignity.
S4.think: I'm frightened, because a robot that picks up floor eggs already exists. That's half my morning, and I'm the slow one.
S4.do: Prays about it, then asks Mr Dawson directly what he's planning. Saves everything, would delay the wedding if needed, and looks at lorry driving or returning to the bakery.
S4.feel: Alarmed, as if the ground he stood on isn't his any more.
S4.quote: Grace's dad would ask why, and I'd have to say I can't promise I can keep her.
S4.fieldNote: His faith comes first in his plan, then a frank talk with his boss. He'd learn the robot if forced, even though he struggles with phones. The wedding, not the job, is what he'd grieve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, no question. What would help is apprenticeships for the new jobs, so men like me can learn on the job and keep earning. Not a payment for staying home, I don't want that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people out here, church is where you'd hear about a job, get a meal, get through a bad year. That counts for more than people in the city think.

headlineQuote: Mr Dawson's son showed me a video and laughed. That's half my morning, and I'm the slow one.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old egg farm worker who got his job through his church elder three years ago and is marrying Grace next summer. He never uses AI, believes in work over handouts, and looks to family, church and community rather than government when times get hard. In the early pictures his worries are for his younger brother and for Grace's bank job, and he'd act fast to help them. The robot picture frightens him because a floor-egg robot already exists, and the thing he dreads most is having to push back his wedding.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because a robot could take his morning work and he'd have to push back his wedding.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships in the new jobs so workers can learn while earning, rather than payments for staying home.
